01 · THE GAME

A city you take one person at a time

In The Suborned, a city carries out your plan without knowing it. A waitress spills a coffee, a guard steps away, a driver takes a different street: each does one small thing for their own reasons, and only you see the whole. They are the Suborned, and you lead the covert cell that turns them. It starts with one favour. By the end, whole streets block the police, lorries ram barricades and crowds fight at your signal. Everyone you turned remembers how, and the city decides whether you are its heroes or its menace.

GenreReal-time tactics · social infiltration
FantasyCommander: plan from above, the city acts
Mission8–12 min on a live clock
Cell4 operatives, one verb each
ReplayHero and Menace campaigns turn different people
TouchstonesSyndicate · Desperados III · Deus Ex · Watch Dogs: Legion · Fable · Shadow of Mordor's Nemesis
Review note. This version answers review of the submitted v0.9.18. The course instructor's feedback was that the GDD read too much like a manual, not the game and the excitement of how it plays. So the GDD leads with the game: sections 01–08 are what you play, the build and the agent crew come after, technical language is kept out, and the detail agents need lives in the agentic design document. What review changed →

Three pillars, one arc

Subvert people

Learn what someone wants and how they are wired, then make an offer that fits.

Test: does knowing more about a person make them cheaper, quieter or more loyal?

Orchestrate the city

Combine contacts, routines and machines into a timed window. Later, into a street that rises on cue.

Test: does it open or close a window the player can see coming?

Live with it

Every method leaves a trace, a reputation and a relationship that grows braver or more bitter.

Test: will the player meet this choice again?

Signature moment. In training you cleared Inez's debt. Over three missions she grows braver, from tipping you off to hiding an operative. In the fourth mission the police close the street, and Inez drives the getaway car through the cordon. In a different playthrough you threatened her instead. She complied every time and grew more resentful, and in the fourth mission she is the one who told the police where you would be.

The world: the 1950s, with centuries of atomic power

The world is an alternate history, not a forecast: "a 1950s world that discovered atomic power centuries ago". Its culture and style are the 1950s; its technology is centuries ahead ("robots have 1950's style, the trams etc, just the technology is super advanced"). It is not the 1950s imagining the year 2000.

  • What atomic power made cheap: energy, travel and building. Sky rail, skyports, towers and liners; everything physical is abundant.
  • What never came: thinking machines and networks ("internet wasn't a thing"). There is no networked computing. Robots are clockwork-smart and follow fixed routines. Records are physical: microfilm, punch cards, pneumatic tubes, stamped forms. Information moves through people and paper, so people are the weak point, and that is why the game is about suborning them (the pillar subvert people, the tiebreaker people over powers).
  • What the city fears most: disorder. An abundant, orderly city runs on routine and paperwork; that is the reason for its optimistic surface and coercive machinery.
  • The design test for every object: 1950s style, centuries-ahead technology. Crossing signals float; road markings need not be paint.
  • How the rules read in it (the rules don't change): cameras are closed-circuit, watched by people; a watcher's log is a physical record that investigators pull; calls are voice between people, by telephone or radio; the "networks" of Act II and of the trams are people and lines, never computers; "no AI during play", fight AI and AI crowd chatter are build terms, not part of the world.

Tiebreakers

  1. Readable over rich. The player can always see who saw what, what it cost and what changed.
  2. People over powers. Access and firepower come through people with motives, never generic abilities.
  3. Systems, not scripts. Nothing is hand-authored. Content is generated, then checked by simulation.
  4. Preparation beats improvisation, both in stealth and in a street fight.
  5. Commander, not avatar. The camera stays above the street. Dropping to street level is a reward, never a way to control the game.
  6. Exteriors only. Interiors are timed actions that happen off screen. Shops, bars and workshops are their frontages: shopfront, canopy, door, service bay.
  7. Many levels, all outside. Street (0), deck (9.43 m) and sky concourse (24 m, where the sky rail stops). Megastructures carry the upper levels; stairs, ramps, escalators and lifts join them.
02 · LOOPS

Watch, turn, time, take, inherit

Watch→Learn→Turn→Time→Take→Fight→Inherit

A chain nobody else sees

Even the training mission is a chain. Each person thinks they are solving their own problem; only you see the whole, and the city then works backward from the result, one link at a time. Later operations chain more links across a district.

What the player manages

ResourceScopeBuys or drivesComes from
CashCampaignFees, debts, bribes. Turning people.Sources (a skimming clerk, a crooked bookmaker)
ArmsCampaignWinning fights. Arming citizens who join you.Sources (a quartermaster, a hijacked shipment)
AssetsCampaignTurned people: access, income, allies in fightsThe Fixer's work, and introductions from other assets
TimeMissionEvery action takes 6–62 s, and scheduled events keep coming—
TrailCampaignInvestigations. Fight frequency, as part of Heat.Traceable acts: threats, conspicuous payments, gunfire
Alert 0–3MissionSecurity's response right nowWitness reports, discovered faults, shots
StandingDistrictWho agrees easily, who refuses, how crowds behaveWitnessed acts only (§04)

Every order shows its full price before you commit: cash, time, Trail and Alert risk.

Fast travel. Boarding a tram or the sky rail takes the cell across the city: board at any stop or station and ride to any other. It costs time only: the wait for the next service plus the ride, both from the timetable. There is no fare. Spec

03 · THE CELL

Four operatives, four verbs

Scout

Watch · Listen · Mislead. Reveals routines, needs and temperament. Can send rivals after false tips.

Fixer

Turn · Call. Makes offers, pays, helps or threatens, then calls contacts in at the right moment. The face everyone remembers.

Tech

Loop · Reroute. Blinds surveillance and misdirects patrols, but stays tethered to the system while it holds. It was a robot in the test; the look follows the era (§10).

Enforcer

Enter · Take · Fire. The only operative who carries the target or shoots. Everyone else works to make this operative's move quiet.

Training gives you the full cell so you learn all four verbs. The campaign starts with the Fixer alone, and recruiting the rest of the cell is the first stretch of progression. Recruits come through the same verbs: turn someone who has the skill. Spec

04 · PEOPLE

Knowledge makes consent cheap. Reputation decides who says yes.

Every person has a routine, a need, a temperament and a memory. What you learn changes the price. Your reputation changes who will even listen.

Four ways to turn someone

Approach (Inez, training)RequiresCashTimeTrailWhat it leaves
Ask coldNothing$025 s+1A refusal that is remembered. Later offers cost +$10,000 and +1 Trail.
PayRoutine known (Watch, 52 s)$70,00050 s+2A traceable payment. The relationship stays neutral.
Help (clear her debt)Need known (Listen, 42 s)$40,00050 s+1Gratitude. Her bravery can grow.
Pressure (threaten)Need known$035 s+3Fear. Her resentment grows, and she can identify the Fixer.

Built These values come from the top-down test. Paying Inez plus turning the driver costs $110,000 against a $100,000 purse. Helping her plus turning the driver costs $80,000. So finding things out is what pays for a second route.

Temperament Spec

TemperamentResponds toIf you are HeroesIf you are a Menace
IdealistHelp. Refuses bribes.Volunteers with no offer needed; gains bravery fastRefuses, and may report you
MercenaryPayOvercharges you: "heroes can afford it"Gives a discount, and sells you out to the highest bidder
FearfulPressureHesitates and needs Help twiceFolds immediately, for free
Loyal (to an institution)Only trust built over timeCan turn after repeated HelpReports any approach

A Hero campaign and a Menace campaign turn different halves of the city, so a second playthrough has a different cast. That's the replay value.

Braver or more bitter

Helped contacts get braver

Informant → Helper → Accomplice → Fighter. They rise one step after each successful job where they were not exposed. An Accomplice hides an operative or drives. A Fighter joins fights armed. Spec

Coerced contacts get bitter

Compliant → Resentful → Informer. They rise one step each time you pressure them or they are exposed. An Informer sells a route to the police or rivals, which schedules an ambush in a later mission. Spec

Talkers, not only turncoats. Every person holds facts: who saw the Fixer's face, who knows the cell's car, who saw where you went and when. Questioned, a person gives up what they know when fear plus resentment outweighs bravery plus loyalty. The rule is fixed, so the same situation always gives the same answer. A contact can stop short of Informer and still fold under questioning. A brave, helped contact lies for you, and investigators get nothing or a false lead. Spec

Contacts also have lives between missions. They can be promoted (new access), arrested (lost unless freed) or introduce a friend (a new contact). The debrief reports each change with its cause.

Standing: heroes or menace

Each district rates you on a Hero ↔ Menace scale, built only from acts people witness. Shielding civilians in a fight, clearing debts in public and freeing arrested locals push toward Hero. Shooting in crowds, public threats and harm to bystanders push toward Menace. An unwitnessed threat moves nothing, though the person you threatened still knows. Neither end loses. They are two ways to control the city:

HeroMenace
Turning peopleSlower and dearer, loyal resultsFaster and cheaper, with betrayal risk
CrowdsJoin your fights and hide your operativesObey out of fear, report when they can, scatter under fire
FightsFewer, and police hesitate in crowdsMore often, and police and rivals come in harder
The street shows itHero graffiti, cheering, free tipsWanted posters, averted eyes, empty pavements
05 · PRESSURE

The city moves without you

Urgency comes from scheduled events with a reason behind them, never from an arbitrary countdown. Each mission defines its own closing event.

Security

  • A guard on a door routine, with a café stop before his shift.
  • Surveillance with fixed, visible cones, blocked by roofs and parked vehicles.
  • A patrol on a sweep, which breaks off toward gunfire within 30 m.
  • A response unit sent on a report. The district seals 2:25 after it arrives. Built

Rivals

  • A rival crew after the same target, on its own schedule. Their Handover schedule is in §07.
  • A false tip sends them away for 3:50. Gunfire brings them within 16 s. Built

Alert, 0 to 3

LevelSecurity doesRaised by
0 · RoutineFollows its schedules—
1 · InquiryChecks the reported spot. The patrol tightens its sweep.A witness report or a discovered fault, counted once per incident Spec
2 · SearchSends the response unit to the reported routeA second incident, or any gunfire (§06) Built
3 · LockdownExterior doors lock, and the district begins to seal.Violence seen by a civilian witness sets 3 at once Built

The crowd is cover and witness Spec

Anyone with a clear line of sight within 13 m of a traceable act becomes a witness, adding +1 Trail per incident and moving Standing. Dense crowds also break the sightlines of guards and cameras. Busy streets are both a hiding place and a risk.

Levels Spec. Sightlines and the 13 m run in three dimensions: a deck blocks sight straight up and down, an open edge does not. People change level only by stair, ramp, escalator or lift, and that takes time. Watchers stand on every level; a station's watcher covers its concourse. A crowded deck above a quiet service lane is a choice the player can see.

Watchers log everyone Spec

Cameras and civic robots stand at key places on the district plan: stations, stops, gates and squares. Anyone in their line of sight is logged with a place and a time, whatever they are doing. Once a Trail is open, investigators can pull the log, and every sighting becomes a lead. If the cell is hot (Heat over its threshold) or its Standing in the district is Menace, a sighting counts as a witness report and raises Alert.

Investigators follow the trail Spec

City management works the streets in real time. Units on foot question someone about every 20 s; cars cover ground fast and stop to question. More come out as Alert and Trail rise. They pick civilians near the last incident by sightline and distance, not by luck. A useful answer is a fact with a place and a time: they go there and question again, closing in lead by lead, roughly 60–90 s per hop.

The player sees it happen: a questioning icon, a dotted line joining the leads they hold, and the unit following it. Counters: keep moving so a sighting goes stale, reach a witness first (pay, reassure or threaten, and threats raise fear), send them the wrong way with the Scout's false tip, block their cars with citizens, or break sightlines in a crowd. What they learn carries into the debrief's Investigation state and the next mission. In a Hero campaign, brave locals feed them false leads.

06 · FIGHTS

The test of how much of the city is yours

Fights are real and grow as you rise. They aren't a separate combat game. They measure your preparation: arms bought, contacts brave enough to stand with you, and streets that decide whose side they are on.

How fights escalate Spec

  • How often depends on Heat = campaign Trail + Menace standing. Crossing a Heat threshold schedules a fight event (a raid, an ambush, a rival hit) in the next mission. No dice.
  • How big depends on the act: 3–6 hostiles in act I, 8–15 in act II, 20–30 in act III. The hard cap is 30 actively simulated combatants. Everyone else is background crowd that can only run or cheer.
  • Your side = cell + Accomplice/Fighter contacts + crowd joiners (Hero standing), armed up to your Arms stock.

What citizens can do

Scatter

Panic that breaks enemy sightlines and covers a retreat.

Block

Park a lorry, stall a tram or fill a street to stop police vehicles.

Join

Fight bare-handed, or armed if you have the Arms.

Vehicle strike

Ram a barricade, or send a rigged vehicle. The driver always jumps clear.

Content line. Civilians are never the payload. A coerced person driving a bomb is a suicide attack, which is a problem for age rating, store listing and press, and a tone the game should not carry. The Menace version can be uglier (collateral damage, witnesses who saw who forced them), but no civilian dies as the weapon.

Syndicate-style fights Spec

Everyone has health, shown as a bar when selected and for everyone in a fight. Starting values: civilian 2, guard or officer 3, rival 3, patrol unit 4, Scout, Fixer and Tech 4, Enforcer 6. Weapons bought with Arms set damage and fire rate, from a pistol (1 damage) to heavier guns (2–3). Armour and healing come through people, not upgrades: a quartermaster supplies armour, a turned doctor heals.

Down, not dead. An operative at 0 is downed. Another operative can carry them to the car; if they are left behind, they are captured, and freeing them becomes a mission.

Anyone can be shot, civilians included. Every civilian who sees it becomes a witness, and Standing moves toward Menace. A contact who witnesses it loses bravery and gains fear and resentment. Some turn Informer; more become Talkers who give you up when questioned (§04). It is the quickest way to undo everything you've built.

Violence has a price

The prototype uses a simple version: each Enforcer shot takes 6 s, two hits drop a person or a patrol unit, and the Enforcer can take three. Every shot adds +1 Alert and +2 Trail, draws rivals and patrols, and moves Standing toward Menace if witnessed. Shooting a contact ends that relationship. Built Faster weapons make going loud more tempting, so playtests decide whether those costs rise.

The decisive shot

No first-person firefights (tiebreaker 5). Instead, once or twice per fight, time slows, the camera drops behind the Enforcer for one aimed shot (the rival leader, a police car's tyre), then returns to the tactical view. After capstone

07 · TRAINING MISSION · CAPSTONE

Handover

Councillor Vale signed the clearance order for the marked block. At shift handover he leaves the Civic Records Office for his official car. Take him alive to the getaway car. The whole cell is available, the purse is $100,000, and every verb is introduced once.

The top-down test in play at 2:39. The Scout has learned Inez’s debt, so the Fixer’s action cards show what each approach costs. Red cones are surveillance and security, amber is the guard, violet the rivals.

Layout and sightlines from the top-down test, which also supplied the art.

Schedule

0:00Vale is inside. The guard, cameras and patrol follow their routines. The cell waits at the getaway car.
3:10The rival car parks near the pickup.
5:40Last chance to turn the driver.
5:50Vale leaves by the north entrance, or the service lane if the driver was turned.
6:10Vale reaches the car.
8:00Rivals take Vale, or the official car leaves. Mission over.

Two routes

A · Through the front door (before 5:50)

  1. Scout watches the café and listens to Inez (1:34).
  2. Fixer helps Inez by clearing her debt ($40,000).
  3. Tech loops the entrance camera (1:02) and stays tethered. Optionally, it reroutes the patrol for 1:55.
  4. Fixer calls Inez. The guard walks 30 s, stays 60 s and walks 30 s back: a 2:00 window. Payoff cut (§10).
  5. Enforcer enters (38 s), leaves with Vale by the service exit and heads for the car (44 s).

B · Take the pickup (from 5:50)

  1. Scout watches the official car: the driver needs cash (48 s).
  2. Fixer turns the driver before 5:40 ($40,000). The pickup moves to the service lane. Or the driver parks across the pickup camera for 2:30.
  3. Scout plants a false tip on the rivals (44 s), or you fight.
  4. Enforcer intercepts (38 s) and heads for the car (44 s).

The final fight: your approach picks your enemy Spec

Every run ends with a short fight on the way to the car, lasting 30–60 s with 3–5 hostiles.

You went loud

Any shot fired, or Alert 2 or higher. The police arrive from the west street with 2–4 officers, and the seal clock is running. There are no allies: the guard is down or against you.

You played it safe

No shots and Alert 1 or lower. The rival crew ambushes the extraction. The guard, who never saw you, fights the rivals attacking his post. A helped Inez warns you 10 s early. A turned driver blocks the rival car, so one fewer rival arrives. An earlier false tip cost them one more member.

Win and fail

Win: Vale reaches the getaway car alive.

Fail: Vale killed · Vale leaves in the official car · rivals reach Vale · the district seals · the Enforcer goes down · the entry is seen by the guard, a live camera or the patrol. Withdrawing ends the attempt.

08 · CAMPAIGN

From one waitress to the city

Act IOne personThe Fixer alone. Turn individuals, recruit the cell and build your first sources of income.
Act IINetworksContacts introduce contacts. Take over a workplace (the docks, a depot). Brave contacts fight beside you.
Act IIIDistrictsStreets rise or obey on cue. Standing decides which. Institutions and rival factions field squads.

People are the economy Spec

A turned person can become a source that pays out every mission: a bank clerk skims cash, a quartermaster diverts arms, a café owner passes on tips that reveal needs before the Scout listens. Procurement missions target a source, not a one-off withdrawal. Resources turn more people, and more people produce more resources. This compounding is the snowball.

Wounds carry over Spec

Health doesn't reset between missions. A turned doctor heals the cell quickly and quietly. Without one, finding a doctor becomes an objective of its own: watch, turn or pay one before the main mission, if the city's calendar leaves time. Nothing forces it. Go in hurt, go in short-handed, or spend the days. The main mission's closing event keeps its date either way, because this is a living city, not a menu.

Objectives vary: a kidnapping, a bank job built on a planted teller, a killing by a manipulated proxy, a takeover won through a ruined reputation. Direct force always works, with a bigger trail. Spec

The debrief writes the next mission Built

OutputStatesComputed from
Public securityCalm → Raised → HighFinal Alert, and whether any shot was fired
InvestigationLittle evidence → Early → Active (named cause)Trail 0 / 1–2 / 3+, with named witnesses taking precedence
AssetsFor example, Inez can introduce café contacts · Inez may identify the FixerHow each contact was turned and what they saw
Standing, bravery and resentment, Heat SpecPer district and per contactWitnessed acts, jobs completed, pressure used

Replay freely before you Continue. After that the result stands, and replays are practice only.

09 · GENERATION

Nothing hand-authored, everything checked

No person, mission or line of dialogue is written by hand. Sky writes the rules and the generators. The simulation plays every generated mission before a player sees it.

ContentGenerated fromChecked by
PeopleOccupation × temperament × need × relationships × routine, fitted to district schedulesAutomatic checks: every person can reach their places and has one clear need
MissionsTemplate (objective, target, closing event, fight trigger) filled with district peopleThe mission checker (below)
Dialogue, portraits, voicesEach person's data plus their state (brave, resentful, promoted), produced at build timeTone and rating filters, plus a sampled review
District plansRoads, transit lines, plots and gates, building and level standards, the trades each area wants and its megastructures, proposed by Datum; block layouts by Vantage; all inside the planning standardsThe plan checker: road hierarchy, gates, track and sky rail standards, walking reach, no dead ends
The built worldA generator fills every plot from the plan's standards, seeded by plot: buildings, towers, roofs, the shops, bars and repair shops along each street, decks, stairs and lifts, and the megastructuresThe plan checker (heights, levels reach the street, megastructures sited, frontages fit). Same plan, same world
ConsequencesThe rules, applied to the mission logReplaying the mission to confirm the same result
The mission checker: a generated mission ships only if at least 2 quiet routes win · a loud route exists and costs more Trail · every way to fail can actually happen · no single contact is essential · a player who knows everything finishes with at least a minute to spare.

The risk is sameness. When everyone is generated, it's easy for nobody to be memorable. Watch Dogs: Legion is the cautionary example. The answer is history, not backstory: people become memorable through what the systems record with you (who you helped, who got braver, who sold you out). Generated text is only a light layer on top.

Build time only. No AI runs during play. The same choices always give the same result, it costs nothing to run, and any mission can be replayed exactly. Live AI crowd chatter can be tried later, as long as it never touches the rules.

10 · PRESENTATION

Read the street at a glance

Camera

A fixed tactical view (play zoom 14 at 38°, never first person) over a 3D city built from the district plan: DecoKit kit pieces where they count, procedural fill to the same bar. Target on-screen character height is 40–60 px at 1080p, enough to read job, silhouette and facing. The rules move across unchanged. Painted plates are at most an optional extra after the capstone. With several levels, architecture above the selected person's level ghosts to 0.2 and keeps 0.4 of its shadow, so the street behind a faded tower is lit and the tower still marks the ground.

Built world or live state

Built world (generated from the plan at build time, fixed in play): buildings, paving, structures, street furniture, skyline. Live 3D state: people, vehicles, doors, surveillance, barricades, posters, and anything that changes state. Both share one material and lighting standard; match lighting on one character and one vehicle before building more.

Control and time

Click to select or move, Shift to group, 1–4 to pick an operative, E to engage, F to fire, C to call. Clicking a person, door or camera opens its action card with the full price. Next Event jumps to the next scheduled change. A live clock with tactical pause, to be settled by playtest. The same orders always give the same result, so pausing never changes the outcome.

Readability

Surveillance cones in security red, the guard in amber, rivals in violet. Signals are drawn unlit and emissive and outside the post grade (the grade shifts them ΔE 4–10), so neither light nor grade shifts them: a signal never depends on the light. Each also has a shape or motion cue. Gameplay signals use colours no environment surface uses at full strength: every world colour stays at least ΔE 20 from each signal, measured on the unlit palette. One exception ("red is definitely ok for electronics displays"): a small emissive pictogram on an electronic display, such as a crossing signal's stop figure, may be red. It is never a surface, and the cones keep their own shape and motion cue. The dossier separates known, suspected and planned.

Payoff cuts

When a plan lands, cut briefly to a street-level camera before returning to the same state. The capstone guarantees one: Inez spills the coffee and the guard walks off. More payoff cuts and the decisive shot come later. Spec

Audio is part of the clock

  • Routines you can hear: a bell, the café door, the handover chime at 5:30.
  • Security warns before it acts: a surveillance click at the edge of each sweep, and a change in the patrol's sound when it breaks route.
  • Alert adds layers to the music. A fight brings in the whole score. Contacts confirm calls aloud.

Look: retro-future, held in the art bible

A bright retro-future city: a 1952–1962 space age imagined as the present, built as high art. It is an alternate history, not a forecast (section 01): a 1950s world that discovered atomic power centuries ago, so its culture and style are the 1950s and its technology is centuries ahead, with no thinking machines or networks. The design test for every object is 1950s style with centuries-ahead technology. A pastel base of cream and peach limestone with saturated enamel accents (cobalt, flamingo, sunshine, mint, turquoise) on panels, awnings, signs, roofs and trim, lagoon water, coral transit, chrome, and a skyline of towers, rockets and planets. It is optimistic on the surface and coercive underneath, and that contrast sets the tone. Citizens wear space-age couture as street clothing; security and institutions dress sleeker in ivory, black, gold and chrome; robots are characters with dot-matrix faces, 1950s in style and clockwork-smart on fixed routines. The four in the cell look like visitors from a nearby timeline: the same world a few decades on, sharper and cleaner, so they pass in the street and still stand out at 50 px. The captures below are the reference. In play, the skyline and distant views frame the edge of the screen while the playable block stays dense and tactical.

The look is set; the palette is current and tuneable. Agent GDD §15 and its machine copy, contracts/style/suborned.style.json (v0.20.0, wins on conflict), hold the palette with hex values, materials, finishes, the hard rules, the reference board and the probe set any new render route must pass. The world palette comes from unity/Assets/Suborned/Editor/World/looks/harbour.json; every colour stays at least ΔE 20 from the three signal colours, measured on the unlit palette. Tuned in the world for v0.18.0: lagoon water #3d8d93, canvas #f7f4ec, and facade accent roles in teal, coral, gold, mint and peach. For v0.19.0 the world gold turns to brass #99784d at street level and on facades (below). Sky reviews it in the world and it can still be tuned. The v0.15.0 art bible is history: a concept look reference, superseded on presentation and palette. Vela, Forma, Glint and Glyph hold §15.

The Harbour District skyline. SpaceHQ is the city's flagship and centrepiece at Crown Circus: the tallest thing in the district, about 252 m, a fluted cream-and-gold tower crowned with an atom over a needle mast, not a rocket. Rival spires stand inland and may be taller than the Skyport (123–194 m, never more than 200); the Skyport, at 108 m, is the harbour's icon, and nothing within 150 m of the quay is taller. Crown Avenue keeps its tower heights, the needle at 167.8 m and the avenue gates at 165.6 m, an exception to the massing grammar's 20 % height variety. Rockets stand only on the horizon, at least 3.2 km out. The sky rail threads buildings and megastructures through portals, and stations also sit inside buildings at the sky concourse. The Parade stays open to the sky: the sky rail passes through the gate block's portal, and glazed barrel canopies run over the side gallery promenades only, never over the carriageway or the play space, so the tactical camera sees the street, its sun and shadows, and the full skyline. The ocean liner at the berth is concept B, "atomic": a flared white hull with a coral boot-top and a gold sheer line, a domed glass observation lounge at the bow, twin swept-back coral tail-fin funnels and a chrome radar mast topped by an atom.

The civic block and the street. The eight concept paintings of 26 September 2026 (briefs/008/concepts/, hashes in PROVENANCE.json) are the reference for the civic block and for the street-level character of the district: cream stone, seafoam teal bands, chrome spheres, banners, planted terraces, pale paving with teal bands, cypress and palms, parasol terraces. The skyline keeps its own reference, the AtomicAge and Blocks sheets. The 30 September capstone concept and its testbed models are not the reference, though their dressing parts may be reused. On the civic block, seafoam #72b5a7 and deep teal #1f6c67 are the kit enamels, with civic wall ivory #eee9da, pale seafoam #9bcfc2 and brass trim #99784d. Banners, flowers and any tram take the palette's coral, flamingo or peach, never the paintings' red-orange, which sits ΔE 8.8 from the cones signal. Brass, not gold, at street level and on facades: brass #99784d and light brass #ad866f, the lightest brass that stays ΔE 20 from the guard amber. The skyline crowns keep their gold (#e3d681, #c9c08e) until a far shot decides. Gold or brass stays hairline, frame, bead and small metal. A large part never takes brass or gold; it takes an enamel, chrome or stone role: the rooftop spheres keep their building's enamel, as roof parts take their host building's enamel pair and the paintings show chrome and pearl spheres, and the two areas that listed gold (lantern and records) take sunshine #f8e26c. Crossings have no landing slab since brief 009 (below), so the landing colour pick is closed; the look role crossing retires when the generator change lands.

Concept art first. "Everything should come from concept art really": look decisions come from concept art generated from an open brief in the world's style ("let the AI concept art come up with its own design"). The ΔE and checker rules gate what the art proposes; they are not the source of options. Every concept generation starts from the style contract's concept_prompt: the era (section 01's premise), the city line of the prompts Sky accepted (briefs/009/concepts/PROVENANCE.json), an avoid list and the rule. A decision taken from art cites the image and its prompt. The tools are the Codex CLI image tool (ChatGPT plan) and Runware (Qwen Image 2.1).

Crossings, as this world builds them. The concepts in briefs/009/concepts/ are the reference. Floating signal orbs ("I do like those eyes"): chrome orbs or small saucers hover over the kerb at each end of a crossing, with a round display on each face showing a walking figure (the stop figure may be red, under the display exception) and a thin beam down to a glowing disc on the paving where people wait. No zebra, no paint, no landing slab: the crossing is light set flush in the road, glowing seafoam bars or rows of light dots in brass frames, with brass dome studs along the kerb edge and seafoam inlay arcs in the paving where the crossing lands. Brass stays a frame line.

In the browser build: the Handover café from the tactical camera and Inez at street level (the view a payoff cut uses). In Unity: a populated DecoKit plaza.

A reskin is still possible. If the city moves to another era, that era must provide: institutions that watch people (cameras, watchmen, informants or switchboards) for the Tech to blind · motor vehicles and dense crowds · jobs you can read from clothing · a respectable surface over a coercive machine · firearms and a plausible way to rig a vehicle.

11 · BUILD

Prove the rules small, then dress them

Built

  • Top-down test of Handover: four operatives, two contacts, security, rivals, shooting, debrief and campaign lock. 28 scenario tests pass.
  • Harbour District 3D world in progress, built from the plan: world generator and export, DecoKit kit pieces plus procedural fill, Unity builder. Handover goes in next, then player actions.
  • City simulation architecture chosen: one C# engine as a Unity-free library.

How it's built

  • The rules live apart from the engine. Everything that happens in the city (a guard leaving, a contact answering) is an event with its conditions, effects and witnesses.
  • Any run can be replayed exactly from its starting state and the player's orders.
  • Unity has to pass the same 28 scenarios as the top-down test before it's trusted.
  • One simulation engine. A Unity-free C# library: Unity runs it live, build tools run it headless. Fixed 10 Hz tick, integer state; a replay is the orders plus checksums.
  • Performance is judged by frame rate at play zoom, not by polygon counts. The target is 60 fps at 1080p on a 15-inch MacBook Air M4 (Mac16,13), the reference machine. It has no fan and a 10-core GPU, so it is measured warm, after several minutes of running, at play zoom with people, vehicles and the simulation in, by a perf harness in a development build. A mid-range PC (an RTX 3060-class GPU with a 6-core CPU) must also pass, as a check, not the bar.

Capstone slice (five weeks)

WeekDeliverableExit check
1Rules proven in the top-down testTwo routes win, and going loud fails at a cost Done
2The rules move into Unity. Handover laid out in the 3D world.28 scenarios pass in Unity
3Cell control, contacts, security, rivals, readability passFirst uncoached playtest
4Final fight (both branches), payoff cut, dossier, event log, debriefNew-player test; freeze the rules
5Tuning, fixes, audio cues. No new systems.Final uncoached gate
Gate. An uncoached player can state the objective and fail conditions, pick an approach because of something they learned, explain its cash, time and Trail cost, complete a chain, say why they fought police rather than rivals (or the reverse), and read what the next mission inherits.

If the schedule slips, cut in this order: crowd witnesses (crowds stay decorative) → patrol reroute → camera-block variant → the police branch of the final fight (rivals only). Always keep both routes, the one payoff cut, the debrief and the gate test.

Beyond the capstone

StageScopeEstimate (one human + agents)
Vertical sliceOne district, 2–3 generated missions, temperament, standing, small fights6–10 weeks
Full gameThree acts, three districts, generated missions, fights up to 30About 12 months

Why these numbers. World-building is fast: the DecoKit city, including a 10,000-citizen stress test, took two days. The long poles are the systems, not the assets: tuning temperament, standing and fights through playtests, and getting the generator to produce missions that pass the checker and still feel distinct. These estimates are replaced by measured velocity after the capstone.

Biggest risks: combat feel and animation (walk and run are all that exist so far) · generated people feeling the same · playtest rounds, which need real players and time. Kept small on purpose: 30-combatant cap (fight readability and AI cost, not rendering; the background crowd can be far larger), vehicles on lanes, three districts, no interiors, no first-person play.

12 · AGENT CREW

One lead, clear owners, named handoffs

Seventeen jobs, each held by a named Anima agent. The job label says what each one does and whom to brief; the name is the agent's identity, which carries across projects. Aster, the lead, manages the other sixteen; Sky is the only human integrator. Agents deliver small, finished pieces of work, and only work that serves the capstone goal goes in.

Assess→Assign→Review→Continue

Aster picks the next objective, gives it to one owner with a clear definition of done, has Suture or Redline review the result, then accepts it or sends it back. Aster handles routine choices and escalates to Sky only for a pillar change, new paid spend, release, destructive action or an unresolved conflict.

One rulebook for everyone. Seventeen agents stay consistent because they all build against one list of everything that can happen in the city: what each event needs, what it changes and who sees it. Keel keeps that list. Missions, schedules and dialogue are checked against it before they reach Unity, so no one can hand over a person with an action the game doesn't have, and Suture replays runs to confirm the results match.

Decisions (v0.20.0)

  • Sky: the world is an alternate history, not a forecast: "a 1950s world that discovered atomic power centuries ago" ("retro future was 1950's but if the world had discovered atomic power hundreds years ago"; "robots have 1950's style, the trams etc, just the technology is super advanced"). It replaces "the 1950s imagining the year 2000" of brief 007's image prompts. Atomic power made energy, travel and building cheap, and everything physical is abundant. Thinking machines and networks never came ("internet wasn't a thing"): robots are clockwork-smart on fixed routines, records are physical, and information moves through people and paper, so people are the weak point. The city fears disorder most, which is the reason for its optimistic surface and coercive machinery. The design test for every object: 1950s style, centuries-ahead technology.
  • Aster: both GDDs and the style contract were checked against the premise, with no hard contradiction. The clear compatible readings are recorded in section 01: closed-circuit cameras watched by people, a watcher's log as a physical record, calls as voice between people, the "networks" as people and transit lines, and the AI terms as build terms ("no AI during play" stays a build rule). Readings that would change a rule went to Sky as questions.
  • Sky: red is allowed on electronic displays ("red is definitely ok for electronics displays"). A small emissive display pictogram, such as a crossing signal's stop figure, may be red; it is never a surface, and the cones keep their own shape and motion cue. It is an exception to the ΔE 20 signal-colour rule for display pictograms only.
  • Sky: concept art first ("everything should come from concept art really"; "let the AI concept art come up with its own design"). Look decisions come from concept art generated from an open brief in the world's style; the ΔE and checker rules gate what the art proposes and are not the source of options. The tools are the Codex CLI image tool (ChatGPT plan) and Runware (Qwen Image 2.1). Every concept generation starts from the style contract's concept_prompt, whose city line is the prompts Sky accepted (briefs/009/concepts/PROVENANCE.json); a decision taken from art cites the image and its prompt.
  • Sky (brief 009): crossings as this world builds them, with briefs/009/concepts/ as the reference. Floating signal orbs ("I do like those eyes"): chrome orbs or small saucers over the kerb at each end, a round display on each face with a walking figure, a thin beam down to a glowing disc where people wait. No zebra, no paint, no landing slab: light set flush in the road (glowing seafoam bars or rows of light dots) in brass frames, brass dome studs along the kerb edge, seafoam inlay arcs where the crossing lands. The landing surface of v0.19.0 goes with the slab, so its colour pick is closed.
  • Fact (brief 008): the reference machine measured is the 15-inch MacBook Air M4 (Mac16,13).

Decisions (v0.19.0)

  • Sky: the eight concept paintings of 26 September 2026 (briefs/008/concepts/, hashes in PROVENANCE.json) are the reference for the civic block and the street-level character of the district: cream stone, seafoam teal bands, chrome spheres, banners, planted terraces, pale paving with teal bands, cypress and palms, parasol terraces. The skyline keeps the AtomicAge and Blocks sheets of brief 007. The 30 September capstone concept and its testbed models are not the reference; their dressing parts may be reused.
  • Sky: on the civic block, seafoam #72b5a7 and deep teal #1f6c67 are the kit enamels, with civic wall ivory #eee9da, pale seafoam #9bcfc2 and civic trim brass #99784d. Banners, flowers and any tram take the palette's coral, flamingo or peach, never the paintings' red-orange (ΔE 8.8 from the cones signal).
  • Sky: brass, not gold, at street level and on facades ("I prefer brass to gold"): brass #99784d and light brass #ad866f, the lightest brass that holds ΔE 20 from the guard; a lighter, yellower brass drifts onto the guard amber. The skyline crowns keep their gold (#e3d681, #c9c08e) until a far shot decides. Gold or brass stays hairline, frame, bead and small metal only; a large part never takes brass or gold; it takes an enamel, chrome or stone role (the rooftop spheres keep their building's enamel; the two areas that listed gold, lantern and records, take sunshine #f8e26c). The paintings show chrome and pearl spheres, and roof parts take their host building's enamel pair. Crossing landings have their own surface; its colour is Sky's open pick (mint #7fd0b8 recommended; #d0c848 today).
  • Sky: Crown Avenue keeps its tower heights: the needle at 167.8 m and the avenue gates at 165.6 m, 13.6 % and 14.8 % under the starburst, an exception to the massing grammar's 20 % height variety. The plan does not change; checker rule K-2 holds every regenerated tower to the tip its order states.
  • Aster: signals also draw outside the post grade, since the grade shifts them ΔE 4–10 (Glint measured the guard 19.0 from shaded stone). A signal must never depend on the light: the fix is the signal, never a darker street. Glyph specifies, Latch builds.
  • Aster (Glint's value): the architecture fade's ghost keeps 0.4 of its shadow, separate from the ghost's own 0.2, so the street behind a faded tower is lit and the tower still marks the ground. Glint tunes it.

Decisions (v0.18.0)

  • Sky: signals (cones, guard and rival markers) render unlit and emissive, each with its shape or motion cue. The ΔE 20 gate applies to the unlit palette against the signal colours.
  • Sky: the performance target is 60 fps at 1080p on a MacBook Air M4, the reference machine (no fan, 10-core GPU), measured warm at play zoom with people, vehicles and the simulation in, by a perf harness in a development build. A mid-range PC (an RTX 3060-class GPU with a 6-core CPU) must also pass, as a check. This replaces the PC-only target set earlier the same day in brief 007: the play camera sees a small slice of the city, so integrated graphics is the bar.
  • Sky: SpaceHQ is the city's flagship and centrepiece at Crown Circus (about 252 m), crowned with an atom over a needle mast, not a rocket. Rockets stay on the horizon, at least 3.2 km out. Spires may be taller than the Skyport: inland rivals reach 123–194 m, while the Skyport (108 m) is the harbour's icon and nothing within 150 m of the quay is taller.
  • Sky: the sky rail threads buildings through portals, and stations also sit inside buildings at the sky concourse.
  • Sky: the Parade stays open to the sky. The sky rail passes through the gate block's portal; glazed barrel canopies run over the side gallery promenades only, never over the carriageway or the play space.
  • Sky: the ocean liner is concept B, "atomic". It replaces the liner that read as a modern cruise ship. Owner: Vela.
  • Sky: the palette is tuned in the world: lagoon water #3d8d93, gold #d0c848, canvas #f7f4ec, and accent roles in teal, coral, gold, mint and peach.

Decisions (v0.17.0)

  • Sky: presentation is 3D. The world is a real city built from the plan; painted plates are at most an optional extra. The camera stays fixed and tactical.
  • Sky: the palette mixes a pastel cream and peach base with saturated enamel accents. It is the current palette and can be tuned once seen in the world.
  • Aster: the DecoKit generator belongs to Vela (pieces, materials, facade detail), with Splice owning the pipeline.
  • Aster: Keel builds and owns the C# simulation library; Latch hosts it in Unity; Redline reviews. Open for Sky: confirm, or have Latch build it to Keel's spec.
  • Aster: Splice keeps the checks and the plan-to-world pipeline. The people and vehicle generator moves to Pulse and the mission rule overlays to Waymark: designers own their generators.

The city is planned before it is dressed: Datum lays out the district and Vantage each block, and Latch builds only a plan that passes, so art dresses a city that already works. Motive and Keel draft the rulebook first, and everyone else works from that draft in parallel while Latch builds the game. The week 3 and 4 playtests can still change the rules, so the rulebook is locked only after week 4.

Budget. Agent work runs inside two existing 20× subscriptions (one Codex, one Claude), which cap usage over time rather than charging per use. Aster watches both and drops optional work when the allowance runs low. Anything paid per use, such as Runware and Meshy credits, is priced before use.
